examples/complex_survey.stat:
# A weighted national survey with a continuous outcome. Proved methods assume simple random
# sampling and refuse it; design-based methods use the weights, strata and clusters.
use models.observational
use sampling
use tests.survey

let survey = cross_sectional(
    n=8000,
    exposure="sugary drinks",
    outcome="waist circumference",
    outcome_scale="continuous",
    survey="weighted",
)
let weighted = survey_linear(
    design=fixed(model=survey),
    null=no_association(model=survey),
    alpha=1/20,
    adjusted_for=["age", "sex", "income"],
)
let checked = verify(typeI(weighted))
examples/paper/fisher_design.stat:
# From the StatClaim article, introduction. Two arms of 50 with a binary
# outcome, compared by a two-sided Fisher exact test at the 5% level.
#
# The check asks Lean to prove the Type I error bound: at most 5% under the
# null, for every common success probability. No data are needed. In the web
# studio the proof says Needs Lean; open the study in Codespaces or run
# statclaim check to build it.
use models.two_arm_binomial
use sampling
use tests.fisher

# Two independent binomial samples of 50.
let study = two_arm_binomial(n_control=50, n_treatment=50)
# Arm sizes fixed before any outcome is seen, which the guarantee needs.
# fisher_adaptive shows what happens without it.
let design = fixed(model=study)
# The null: both arms have the same success probability.
let null = equal_proportions(model=study)
# Fisher's exact test, two-sided, at level 1/20.
let analysis = fisher(design=design, null=null, alpha=1/20)

# The claim: Type I error at most the level. Naming it lets you inspect it
# before anything runs.
let claim = typeI(analysis)
# Verified: proved in Lean for every success probability from 0 to 1, with a
# certificate that can be replayed.
let verification = verify(claim)
examples/paper/fisher_observed.stat:
# From the StatClaim article, "Composing models and naming claims". Analysing
# observed counts: 12 of 50 successes in the control arm, 24 of 50 in the
# treatment arm.
#
# calculate proposes the p-value and the decision. verify has Lean check that
# this p-value is exactly the one Fisher's test defines for these counts. In
# the web studio verify says Needs Lean; the calculation runs.
use models.two_arm_binomial
use sampling
use tests.fisher

let study = two_arm_binomial(n_control=50, n_treatment=50)
let design = fixed(model=study)
let null = equal_proportions(model=study)
let analysis = fisher(design=design, null=null, alpha=1/20)

# The observed counts, checked against the design: each lies between 0 and its
# arm size.
let data = observe(analysis=analysis,
                   control_successes=12, treatment_successes=24)
# The claim that a result is correct for these counts.
let observed = result(data)
# p-value about 0.0213, so the null is rejected at 5%. A calculation, not a
# proof, and it does not show that the null is false.
let computation = calculate(observed)
# Verified: Lean checks the exact p-value and the decision against their
# definitions, and issues a certificate.
let checked_result = verify(observed)
# Another name for the same result; verification does not run again.
let saved = checked_result
# Read from the calculation once checks run: 1255807221238/58971773773923.
let p_value = computation.calculation.p_value
# The certificate's file, present only once verify has succeeded.
let certificate = checked_result.evidence.certificate.file
examples/paper/simon_design.stat:
# From the StatClaim article, "Rechecking Simon's two-stage designs". The first
# optimal design in Simon (1989): a single-arm trial with a binary response that
# can stop early for futility.
#
# Lean proves the complete two-stage policy's error bound for every response
# rate up to 5%, and its power at 25%. In the web studio verify says Needs
# Lean; open the study in Codespaces or run statclaim check.
use designs.two_stage
use planning

# Stage one enrols 9; stage two adds 15, for 24 in all (n1 = 9, n = 24).
let stages = two_stage_binomial(n_stage1=9, n_stage2=15)
# Stop after stage one if no one responds (r1 = 0). Otherwise reject the null
# when more than 2 of the 24 respond (r = 2).
let rule = threshold_rule(continue_above=0, reject_above=2)
# The null: a response rate of 5% or less.
let analysis = two_stage_test(design=stages, rule=rule,
                              null_rate=1/20)
# The target: power at least 90% at a response rate of 25%, Type I error at
# most 10%.
let target = power_target(at=response_rate(value=1/4),
                          minimum=9/10, maximum_typeI=1/10)
# Verified: Type I error 0.0931 at 5% and power 0.9028 at 25%. The expected
# size under the null is 14.5.
let checked = verify(meets(analysis=analysis, target=target))
examples/paper/simon_search.stat:
# From the StatClaim article, "Rechecking Simon's two-stage designs". Instead of
# checking a given design, search for one: the optimal and minimax designs with
# at most 120 participants.
#
# The searches return Simon's tabulated designs. The ranking is calculated, not
# proved. In the web studio verify says Needs Lean; the searches run.
use designs.two_stage
use planning

# The design from simon_design: 9 + 15 participants, r1 = 0, r = 2.
let stages = two_stage_binomial(n_stage1=9, n_stage2=15)
let rule = threshold_rule(continue_above=0, reject_above=2)
let analysis = two_stage_test(design=stages, rule=rule,
                              null_rate=1/20)
# Power at least 90% at a response rate of 25%, Type I error at most 10%.
let target = power_target(at=response_rate(value=1/4),
                          minimum=9/10, maximum_typeI=1/10)
# Verified, as in simon_design.
let checked = verify(meets(analysis=analysis, target=target))

# Every design with at most 120 participants, ranked by expected size under the
# null (optimal).
let optimal_candidates = two_stage_designs(null_rate=1/20,
                            max_total=120, criterion="optimal")
# Simon's optimal design: 9 + 15, r1 = 0, r = 2, expected size 14.55.
let optimal = calculate(sample_size(candidates=optimal_candidates,
                                    target=target))
# The same designs, ranked by their largest total size (minimax).
let minimax_candidates = two_stage_designs(null_rate=1/20,
                            max_total=120, criterion="minimax")
# Simon's minimax design: 13 + 7, r1 = 0, r = 2, expected size 16.41. Replace
# calculate with verify to prove that a chosen design meets its targets; the
# ranking stays a calculation.
let minimax = calculate(sample_size(candidates=minimax_candidates,
                                    target=target))
examples/tutorial/02_reading_results.sta:
# Lesson 2: name the parts of a result.
use models.two_arm_binomial
use sampling
use tests.fisher

let study = two_arm_binomial(n_control=50, n_treatment=50)
let analysis = fisher(design=fixed(model=study), null=equal_proportions(model=study), alpha=1/20)
let verification = verify(typeI(analysis))

let status = verification.status
let evidence = verification.evidence
let assumptions = verification.evidence.required_assumptions
let level = analysis.alpha
replication/comparison/graph.stat:
# Three one-sided tests. Two start with half the level and none with the rest; a
# rejected test passes its whole level on, in the cycle first -> second -> third -> first.
#
# StatClaim's side of graph_graphicalMCP.R. The check gives cited: StatClaim
# checks the declared graph before any data exist and cites the procedure's
# familywise bound. statclaim_side.py also runs four broken copies of this
# graph, and StatClaim refuses each. In the web studio the check says Needs
# Lean; run statclaim check for its result.
use models.two_arm_continuous
use sampling
use tests.t
use multiplicity.graphical

let study = two_arm_continuous(n_control=300, n_treatment=300)
let plan = fixed(model=study)
# Three one-sided t-tests, each at 2.5%: two non-inferiority tests with a
# margin of -5 and one superiority test.
let first = t_test_one_sided(design=plan, null=mean_difference_at_most(model=study, value=-5), alpha=1/40)
let second = t_test_one_sided(design=plan, null=mean_difference_at_most(model=study, value=-5), alpha=1/40)
let third = t_test_one_sided(design=plan, null=mean_difference_at_most(model=study, value=0), alpha=1/40)

# Weights are each test's starting share of the level; row i of transitions
# says where test i's level goes once it is rejected.
let procedure = graphical(
    analyses=[first, second, third],
    weights=[1/2, 1/2, 0],
    transitions=[
        [0, 1, 0],
        [0, 0, 1],
        [1, 0, 0],
    ],
    alpha=1/40,
)
# Cited: the familywise error is at most 2.5% whichever nulls are true, as long
# as each test keeps its own level.
let error = verify(familywise(procedure))
replication/comparison/two_arm_power.sta:
# 100 per arm, a true difference of 0.4 standard deviations, two-sided 5%. The same
# design as declaredesign_two_arm.R, whose estimator is a Welch-type difference in means.
#
# Power is 0.807 by a normal formula, and the Welch test's error bound is cited,
# a large-sample result. In the web studio the power runs and the error check
# says Needs Lean.
use models.two_arm_continuous
use sampling
use tests.t
use planning

let study = two_arm_continuous(n_control=100, n_treatment=100)
let analysis = welch_test(design=fixed(model=study), null=equal_means(model=study), alpha=1/20)
let target = power_target(at=mean_difference(value=2/5, sd=1), minimum=4/5, maximum_typeI=1/20)
# Power about 0.807, above the 80% target. A normal approximation, not a bound.
let power = calculate(meets(analysis=analysis, target=target))
# Cited: the error rate approaches 5% as the arms grow; no bound is claimed at
# 100 per arm.
let error = verify(typeI(analysis))
replication/copd/design_cited.stat:
# NCT03162055 (study D5970C00002): glycopyrronium/formoterol (GFF) versus
# umeclidinium/vilanterol (UV) in COPD. Statistical analysis plan, edition 2.0,
# 8 June 2018. The whole multiplicity structure of sections 4.2.6.3 and 4.2.7.1.
#
# The plan analyses continuous endpoints with a mixed model for repeated measures
# and the binary endpoint with logistic regression (sections 4.2.6 and 4.2.7).
# Both are cited tests here.
#
# Running it gives cited for the co-primary family, conditional for the whole
# sequence and cited for the onset test; the file reports cited, its weakest
# part. In the web studio these checks say Needs Lean; open the study in
# Codespaces or run statclaim check.
use models.two_arm_continuous
use models.two_arm_binomial
use sampling
use tests.mixed_model
use tests.logistic
use multiplicity.graphical
use multiplicity.fixed_sequence

# About 440 per arm are expected in the per-protocol set, 500 in the full set.
let per_protocol = two_arm_continuous(n_control=440, n_treatment=440)
let full_set = two_arm_continuous(n_control=500, n_treatment=500)
let full_set_binary = two_arm_binomial(n_control=500, n_treatment=500)

# Co-primary hypotheses (section 4.1.1). Non-inferiority uses the per-protocol
# set with a margin of -50 mL; superiority uses the full set.
let trough_fev1_ni = mmrm_test_one_sided(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-50),
    alpha=1/40,
)
let peak_fev1_ni = mmrm_test_one_sided(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-50),
    alpha=1/40,
)
let peak_fev1_sup = mmrm_test_one_sided(
    design=fixed(model=full_set),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=full_set, value=0),
    alpha=1/40,
)

# Section 4.2.6.3: 1.25% each to the two non-inferiority tests, recycled
# trough NI -> peak NI -> peak superiority -> trough NI.
let co_primary = graphical(
    analyses=[trough_fev1_ni, peak_fev1_ni, peak_fev1_sup],
    weights=[1/2, 1/2, 0],
    transitions=[
        [0, 1, 0],
        [0, 0, 1],
        [1, 0, 0],
    ],
    alpha=1/40,
)

# Section 4.2.7.1: secondary endpoints in this order at one-sided 2.5%.
let inspiratory_capacity_ni = mmrm_test_one_sided(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-50),
    alpha=1/40,
)
let onset_of_action_sup = logistic_regression_one_sided(
    design=fixed(model=full_set_binary),
    null=proportion_difference_at_most(model=full_set_binary, value=0),
    alpha=1/40,
)
let tdi_ni = mmrm_test_one_sided(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-1),
    alpha=1/40,
)
# EMSCI severity score, margin -0.1, encoded as written: higher scores count
# as better. The plan does not say which direction is better, so the report
# lists higher_is_better as an assumption.
let emsci_ni = mmrm_test_one_sided(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-1/10),
    alpha=1/40,
)

# "Should all 3 null hypotheses relating to the co-primary endpoints be rejected
# then testing will proceed to the secondary endpoints."
let trial = fixed_sequence(
    analyses=[co_primary, inspiratory_capacity_ni, onset_of_action_sup, tdi_ni, emsci_ni],
    alpha=1/40,
)

# Cited: the graphical procedure's familywise bound comes from the literature,
# and its tests are cited mixed models, so the bound is a large-sample one.
let primary_error = verify(familywise(co_primary))
# Conditional: Lean proves that the sequence keeps the familywise error at 2.5%
# if each member keeps its own. The members' guarantees are assumed, so the
# scope stays large-sample.
let overall_error = verify(familywise(trial))
# Cited: the logistic regression's error bound is a large-sample result.
let onset_error = verify(typeI(onset_of_action_sup))
replication/copd/design_declared.stat:
# NCT03162055 (study D5970C00002): glycopyrronium/formoterol (GFF) versus
# umeclidinium/vilanterol (UV) in COPD. Statistical analysis plan, edition 2.0,
# 8 June 2018. The whole multiplicity structure of sections 4.2.6.3 and 4.2.7.1.
#
# Each analysis is declared by name, with the plan's section as its reference.
# StatClaim checks nothing about these tests themselves.
#
# Running it gives cited for the co-primary family, whose graphical procedure
# is a cited method over declared tests, and conditional for the whole
# sequence; the file reports declared, its weakest part. In the web studio
# these checks say Needs Lean; open the study in Codespaces or run statclaim
# check.
use models.two_arm_continuous
use models.two_arm_binomial
use sampling
use tests.declared
use multiplicity.graphical
use multiplicity.fixed_sequence

# About 440 per arm are expected in the per-protocol set, 500 in the full set.
let per_protocol = two_arm_continuous(n_control=440, n_treatment=440)
let full_set = two_arm_continuous(n_control=500, n_treatment=500)
let full_set_binary = two_arm_binomial(n_control=500, n_treatment=500)

# Co-primary hypotheses (section 4.1.1). Non-inferiority uses the per-protocol
# set with a margin of -50 mL; superiority uses the full set.
let trough_fev1_ni = declared_test(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-50),
    alpha=1/40,
    method="Mixed model for repeated measures, treatment contrast over 24 weeks",
    reference="Statistical analysis plan edition 2.0, section 4.2.6.1",
)
let peak_fev1_ni = declared_test(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-50),
    alpha=1/40,
    method="Mixed model for repeated measures, treatment contrast over 24 weeks",
    reference="Statistical analysis plan edition 2.0, section 4.2.6.2",
)
let peak_fev1_sup = declared_test(
    design=fixed(model=full_set),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=full_set, value=0),
    alpha=1/40,
    method="Mixed model for repeated measures, treatment contrast over 24 weeks",
    reference="Statistical analysis plan edition 2.0, section 4.2.6.2",
)

# Section 4.2.6.3: 1.25% each to the two non-inferiority tests, recycled
# trough NI -> peak NI -> peak superiority -> trough NI.
let co_primary = graphical(
    analyses=[trough_fev1_ni, peak_fev1_ni, peak_fev1_sup],
    weights=[1/2, 1/2, 0],
    transitions=[
        [0, 1, 0],
        [0, 0, 1],
        [1, 0, 0],
    ],
    alpha=1/40,
)

# Section 4.2.7.1: secondary endpoints in this order at one-sided 2.5%.
let inspiratory_capacity_ni = declared_test(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-50),
    alpha=1/40,
    method="Mixed model for repeated measures, treatment contrast over 24 weeks",
    reference="Statistical analysis plan edition 2.0, section 4.2.7.2",
)
let onset_of_action_sup = declared_test(
    design=fixed(model=full_set_binary),
    null=proportion_difference_at_most(model=full_set_binary, value=0),
    alpha=1/40,
    method="Logistic regression, treatment coefficient",
    reference="Statistical analysis plan edition 2.0, section 4.2.7.3",
)
let tdi_ni = declared_test(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-1),
    alpha=1/40,
    method="Mixed model for repeated measures, treatment contrast over 24 weeks",
    reference="Statistical analysis plan edition 2.0, section 4.2.7.4",
)
# EMSCI severity score, margin -0.1, encoded as written: higher scores count
# as better. The plan does not say which direction is better, so the report
# lists higher_is_better as an assumption.
let emsci_ni = declared_test(
    design=fixed(model=per_protocol),
    null=mean_difference_at_most(model=per_protocol, value=-1/10),
    alpha=1/40,
    method="Mixed model for repeated measures, treatment contrast over 24 weeks",
    reference="Statistical analysis plan edition 2.0, section 4.2.7.5",
)

# "Should all 3 null hypotheses relating to the co-primary endpoints be rejected
# then testing will proceed to the secondary endpoints."
let trial = fixed_sequence(
    analyses=[co_primary, inspiratory_capacity_ni, onset_of_action_sup, tdi_ni, emsci_ni],
    alpha=1/40,
)

# Cited: the graphical procedure's familywise bound comes from the literature;
# it assumes the declared tests' own bounds.
let primary_error = verify(familywise(co_primary))
# Conditional: Lean proves that the sequence keeps the familywise error at 2.5%
# if each member keeps its own; those guarantees are assumed.
let overall_error = verify(familywise(trial))
